newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi army admits killing 50 Hutu civilians.
newsitem.headline: Burundi army admits killing 50 Hutu civilians.

text.p: Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army admitted on Monday its soldiers killed some 50 Hutu civilians in the southern province of Bururi and said soldiers responsible would be punished.
A senior human rights worker said the rare admission was part of a drive by the army, which seized power on July 25, to clean up its image to try to win over Burundi's Hutu majority.
Aid workers said more than 100 people were killed by the army at Bururi's Matana commune on October 13.

"On October 13 some indisciplined military killed civilians whom they accused of feeding the assailants (rebels) but there was no proof that they were feeding the rebels," said army spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Isaie Nibizi.
"The figures are not clear but around 50 people were killed."
"These killings are regrettable. Our objective is to get the population on our side, not to kill them," Nibizi said, adding arrests had been made and those responsible would be punished.

Foreign aid workers say more than 100 civilians, mainly Hutu women and children, were summarily executed by the army after the civilians went from Bururi's Muzenga zone to the market at Matana to buy beans.
The Hutus were accused of buying supplies for rebels, arrested in two groups and taken to a military camp, they said.
"They released 10 Tutsis but the rest were killed at the military camp and their bodies thrown into the Migerere river," a foreign aid worker said.
More than 150,000 people have been killed in three years of massacres and civil war between the Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels.
Human rights reports have accused the army of killing Hutu civilians indiscriminately while in pursuit of suspected Hutu rebels, a charge denied by the army.
They say the rebels are also guilty of reprisal mass killings of civilians.
Human rights officials and diplomats say despite glaring exceptions the army's record has improved since the coup.

"The situation with human rights is much better but that is partly because the militia are no longer active," Christophe Sebubandi, president of the Burundian League for Human Rights (Iteka), told Reuters.

Diplomats say the army trusts President Pierre Buyoya, a retired army major who ousted civilian Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, enough to allow him to take steps necessary to improve military discipline.

"Now the army has a president that they trust who will let them off the leash as far as fighting the rebels is concerned. But there are also large groups within the army who recognise it cannot win the civil war (by warfare alone)," a diplomat said.
Burundi has been under sanctions imposed by regional states since July 31. The states are demanding immediate peace talks between Buyoya and all other factions including Hutu rebels.
